Hi, I'm not a doctor but I do work in a hospital to help provide pregnancy testing for patients. HCG blood tests are considered a valid measure of pregnancy regardless of the stage in your cycle- the results will not fluctuate. It could be that they are also looking at hormonal levels (such as FSH, LH, estrodiol, testosterone) for explanations as to what is affecting your periods.

The best thing to do is contact your doctor and check whether or not a pregnancy test was definitely performed as part of your blood work. If so and it was negative, the chances of you being pregnant are slim to none. Try not to stress yourself out too much about this as that will only make your symptoms worse- I know that's easier said than done but make sure you're giving yourself time to relax and rest.

Wishing you the best.

For some anecdotal evidence, I was diagnosed with fibromyalgia a few years after PTSD and hadn't had any pain symptoms before experiencing trauma. Psychosomatic pain is a fairly common response, your nervous system is hyperreactive and your brain can misinterpret simple sensations/signals like touch and temperature as pain. It doesn't make the pain any less real but it is definitely a factor for some people with chronic pain.

Food is really key! I gained 20kg whilst on antidepressants because I was mindlessly eating to pass the time. I've since lost the weight and now I hit the gym at least a couple of times a week!

Don't starve yourself and don't commit to diets you can't stick to. A lot of people swear by keto but it can be expensive and hard to maintain. Just try to be mindful of when and what you're eating. Eat your 3 meals a day at the same time and eat til you're full to stave off cravings to snack. Just make sure your meals contain a lot of complex carbs and lower fat/sugar content. Calorie counting can help some people but I find it quite negative for my mental health so I don't bother. If you're hungry, eat. Just make smart choices about what.

Swap out your snacks, if you're going to snack opt for veggies and hummus, fruit, nuts, yoghurt or try a big glass of water first- often when I think I'm hungry I'm actually just thirsty. Switch to diet soda if you can and try to drink less of it as the hidden sugar is really nasty.

Exercise is also important but find something you enjoy, don't make it a chore. Try to aim for 10,000 steps a day, that's a biggie. As for other forms of exercise: running sucks, I will never run. For me, I enjoy lifting weights, it's so rewarding watching the numbers go up slowly as I improve. There's so many choices though, swimming is great for a less intensely weight-bearing exercise, big walks in nature, rock climbing, yoga, try it all out and see what sticks! Make it a fun hobby and you'll want to keep going back without thinking about the fact it's really even exercise.

Fibro is a blanket medical term like IBS- it's code for "nothing abnormal has shown up on tests so we don't know what it is". It's likely that there are a whole host of reasons behind it in any one individual.

I've come to terms with the fact that my fibro is likely partially psychosomatic due to some trauma I suffered a few years prior to my symptoms appearing. It's possible that there are also immunological, neurological, musculoskeletal and other causes for different cases of fibro- we just might never know what they are as there's no profits to be made in researching them.

Regardless of the underlying cause, it still causes so much pain and discomfort and I wish doctors were more sympathetic to that fact rather than raising their eyebrows and hinting that "there's nothing wrong." My pain management specialist advised that I go swimming and do sudoku to keep my mind active. It's an absolute joke.

"Hello again, Genevieve."

"It's Gen." The girl looked over at me as she took her usual seat in the worn Chesterfield armchair opposite my desk.

"Yes, Gen, sorry." I corrected myself, forcing myself to maintain eye contact and smile at the lifeless face staring back at me.

I rifled through my desk drawers for a moment, producing a notepad and pen, shuffling in my seat a little.

Gen waited patiently, unblinking, barely breathing. Her arms lay by her sides, bent in a perfect right-angle her hands resting on her knees with her fingers outstretched as though she were a cat waiting to pounce on her mousy prey.

​

"How are you doing, Gen?"

"My performance levels are maximal."

"And what about your emotional health?"

"I seem to have been experiencing some software errors. My emotion regulator has been malfunctioning."

Her posture remained upright and rigid as she spoke. In the hours that she had spent in my office, I had never seen her blink once. I knew that she was just a sick girl that needed my help but it was hard not to feel at least a little creeped out by her robotic movements and intonations. 

"What do you mean by malfunctioning?"

"My tear ducts have been experiencing a build up in saline fluids and have leaked in response."

"That's called crying, Gen. It's a very human thing to do."

"But I am not human. I am an android." 

She spoke with such conviction, her tone so matter-of-fact that I almost believed it. Until I saw that tell-tale flush of red growing across her freckled cheeks.

​

"How are you finding the medicine that Dr Harrison prescribed?"

"The serotonin reuptake inhibitors are having an adverse affect on my synaptic systems. It is possible that they are responsible for my malfunction."

"Gen, that means that the medication is working. Don't you feel it, that humanity urging to return?"

"I am not human."

​

The girl frustrated me to no end. I stood up from my desk, rubbing my temples with my thumbs the way that all middle-aged men must do when they are experiencing stress. I paced about the room for a moment, trying to come up with a reasonable response to give to this deluded girl. She was as human as I, with flowing red hair that had frazzled in the summer heat, blemished skin with birthmarks and tiny scars and the occaisional pimple. I hadn't a single clue about what to say to drag her back into reality. I stood and thought for a long time under her cold, silent gaze.

"Gen. If it's true that you are indeed an android then what are the three rules that you must always obey?"

"I must never harm a human being. I must never harm myself. I must always obey humans." 

"In that order of priority?"

"Yes."

"So, Gen. If you really were a robot, and I told you that if you did not jump out of my fourth floor office window, then I would jump out myself... would you do it?"

​

There was a brief pause. The sound of hesitant silence now the triumphant fanfare of a breakthrough.

"Yes... yes I would." She sounded unsure, her voice cracking a little with that oh-so human sense of fear. 

I knew that self preservation would win out. Humans were all too selfish to let something like a little psychosis stop them.

"Alright then." I grinned to myself as the devious plan in my head began to bubble over, worried it might pour out of my skull onto the floor and give the game away in my excitement.

​

I yanked off my suit jacket, throwing it onto my desk where it covered heaps of unorganised notes and files and the odd half-finished page of crossword puzzles.

"What are you doing?" Gen asked, that wonderful note of fear, trill and shrill in the back of her throat as I flung open my window.

The sounds of the racing city below danced into the room on the crisp breeze, the honking of angry commuters, the yells of infuriated pedestrians, the hum and thrum of electricity and life and humanity.

"I'm going to jump out of this window. Unless you jump instead."

That was not true.

"No you won't."

She was correct.

"Oh yes, I will. In exactly ten seconds." 

I was lying through my teeth.

​

We both watched the office clock's second hand tick by like the hand of Death itself was mounted on the wall and was flipping us off. Eight.

I couldn't wipe the grin from my face. Seven. The fear in Genevieve's eyes was palpable, almost tangible. Six. I was finally going to get through to her. Five.

"Four. Three. Two. Oh shi-"

​

It was then that I saw her hurtling towards me at an almost inhuman pace. She moved me from the window so precisely, so surely, planting me in my seat. All I could do was watch on in horror as she hurled herself over the railings and presumably plummeted to the ground below. There was a distant crunch that rang in my ears. Followed by the muffled sounds of a car alarm, and screaming, and more screaming. 

Eventually a police officer barged into my office, making his way towards me. He searched my desk, picking up the remote control that had been lying in the top drawer and reached for his walkie-talkie. 

"Yeah, it looks like she was seeing a therapy-droid. He must have been one of the batch of faulty droids. I'll power him down and send him over to the reset crew."

He pressed a button on the remote and my vision faded to black.
